sentences.t:
Heht ðā þæt heaðoweorc tō hagan bīodan
ūp ofer ecgclif, þǣr þæt eorlweorod
morgẹnlongne dæg mōdgiōmor sæt,
bordhæbbende, bēga on wēnum,
endedōgọres ond eftcymes
lēofes monnes.
sentences.l: He bade then that battle-work be proclaimed to the enclosure, up over the edge-cliff, where that earl-troop sat the morning-long day, sad-minded, shield-having, in expectation of both: of the end-day and of the return of the dear man.
sentences.i: Then he ordered the news of the fighting to be carried to the camp, up over the cliff’s edge, where the band of warriors had sat all the morning long, heavy at heart, their shields at hand, looking for one of two things: the last day of the man they loved, or his coming back.
sentences.n: ‘Heht’ is the past of ‘hātan’ (‘bid, command’) with the infinitive ‘bīodan’ (‘proclaim’); neither the one who bids nor the one bidden is named. After Wīglāf’s speech that closes the previous part I take Wīglāf as the one who bids; that is an inference. The man bidden to carry the news is presumably the messenger whose speech follows. ‘Þæt heaðoweorc’ is ‘that battle-work’, the result of the fight; ‘tō hagan’ is ‘to the enclosure’ (‘haga’, a fenced place), which I take as the place where the troop waits (a guess). ‘Ecgclif’ is ‘edge-cliff’; Kemble and four other editors read ‘ēgclif’, which I take as a cliff at the water (I read ‘ēg-’ as ‘water’; a guess). In ‘þǣr þæt eorlweorod … sæt’ the accusative ‘morgẹnlongne dæg’ gives the time, ‘the morning-long day’. The dot under the ‘e’ of ‘morgẹnlongne’ is Klaeber’s sign that the vowel does not count in the metre, so the vowel is scanned as if it were absent; it changes nothing in the sense, and ‘endedōgọres’ has another. ‘Bēga on wēnum’ is ‘in expectation of both’: ‘wēn’ takes the genitive, and ‘bēga’ is the genitive of ‘bēgen’; the two things are ‘endedōgọres ond eftcymes’, ‘of the end-day and of the return’, of ‘lēofes monnes’, ‘the dear man’, who is Beowulf.

sentences.t:
Lȳt swīgode
nīwra spella sē ðe næs gerād,
ac hē sōðlīce sægde ofer ealle:
sentences.l: Little did he keep silent of new tidings, he who rode the headland, but he spoke truly over all:
sentences.i: The man who had ridden over the headland held back little of the new tidings, but told the truth before them all:
sentences.n: ‘Lȳt swīgode nīwra spella’ is ‘little he kept silent of new tidings’: ‘swīgode’ is the past of ‘swīgian’, which takes the genitive (‘spella’, plural of ‘spell’, ‘tidings’), and ‘lȳt’ is ‘little’, a way of saying he held back almost nothing. ‘Sē ðe næs gerād’ names the speaker. I take ‘næs’ as the accusative of ‘næs’ (‘headland’) and ‘gerād’ as the past of ‘gerīdan’ (‘ride’), so ‘he who rode the headland’; that is a guess, because ‘næs’ can also be ‘ne wæs’ (‘was not’), and I cannot construe ‘gerād’ as an adjective after it. ‘Ofer ealle’ is ‘over all’, I take it as ‘in the hearing of all’. The colon opens the speech, and its opening quotation mark stands at the next line.

sentences.l: ‘Now is the wish-giver of the Weders’ people, the lord of the Geats, fast on his death-bed; he dwells in the slaughter-rest through the worm’s deeds;
sentences.i: ‘Now the lord of the Geats, who gave the Weder people their wishes, lies held fast upon his deathbed; he abides in his bed of slaughter, by the dragon’s deeds;
sentences.n: The messenger’s speech begins here and runs past the end of this part. The subject of ‘is … fæst’ and of ‘wunað’ is ‘wilgeofa Wedra lēoda’, ‘wish-giver of the Weder people’, with ‘dryhten Gēata’, ‘lord of the Geats’, in apposition: Weders and Geats are two names for one people, and the king is Beowulf. I take the first element of ‘wilgeofa’ as ‘willa’ (‘wish’), ‘giver of what is wished’; the meaning of the compound is a guess. ‘Dēaðbedde fæst’ is ‘fast to a death-bed’ (‘fæst’ takes the dative). ‘Wunað wælreste’ is ‘dwells in slaughter-rest’, ‘wælreste’ a dative of ‘wælrest’ (‘wæl’ ‘the slain’ + ‘rest’), the resting-place of the slain. ‘Wyrmes dǣdum’ is ‘through the worm’s deeds’, a dative plural of means; ‘wyrm’ is ‘worm’ in ‘l’ and ‘dragon’ in ‘i’ by the house rule.

sentences.t:
him on efn ligeð ealdorgewinna
sexbennum sēoc;
sentences.l: Beside him lies the life-adversary, sick with knife-wounds;
sentences.i: Beside him lies his mortal enemy, stricken with knife-wounds;
sentences.n: ‘Him on efn’ is ‘beside him’ (‘on efn’, ‘level with, alongside’; ‘him’ dative) and ‘ligeð’ is ‘lies’. ‘Ealdorgewinna’ is ‘life-adversary’ (‘ealdor’ ‘life’ + ‘gewinna’ ‘one who strives’): the dragon, who fought Beowulf for his life. ‘Sēoc’ is ‘sick’ and takes the dative ‘sexbennum’, ‘with knife-wounds’: ‘sex-’ is a spelling of ‘seax’ (‘knife’) and ‘bennum’ is the dative plural of ‘benn’ (‘wound’, as in the house ‘feorhbennum’). The italic ‘e’ is Klaeber’s: the manuscript has ‘siex’; Kemble and others print ‘seax-’, Holthausen and Sedgefield ‘sex-’, and every spelling means the knife. I take it to be the knife Beowulf drew in his last stroke (the house ‘wæll-seaxe’, ‘slaughter-knife’).

sentences.t:
sweorde ne meahte
on ðām āglǣcean ǣnige þinga
wunde gewyrcean.
sentences.l: with a sword he could not, upon the awesome one, in any way work a wound.
sentences.i: with the sword he could work no wound at all upon the dragon.
sentences.n: ‘Sweorde’ is a dative of means, ‘with a sword’; ‘meahte’ is the past of ‘magan’ (‘be able’) with the infinitive ‘gewyrcean’ (‘work, make’). The subject is not stated; it is Beowulf, as the sense shows. ‘Ǣnige þinga’ is ‘in any way’ (‘þinga’ is a genitive plural of ‘þing’ used as an adverb, ‘in any things’). ‘Ne’ with ‘ǣnige’ is an emphatic ‘no … at all’; the wounds the dragon bears are those named a few words before, in the same line, from the knife. ‘On ðām āglǣcean’ is ‘upon the awesome one’; ‘āglǣca’ is the disputed word the house renders ‘awesome one’, here the dragon.

sentences.t:
Wīglāf siteð
ofer Bīowulfe, byre Wīhstānes,
eorl ofer ōðrum unlifigendum,
healdeð higemǣðum hēafodwearde
lēofes ond lāðes.
sentences.l: Wīglāf sits over Beowulf, the son of Wīhstān, an earl over others, the not-living; he holds head-watch with mind-reverence of the dear one and the hateful one.
sentences.i: Wīglāf, son of Wīhstān, sits beside Beowulf, one warrior beside the lifeless; with due reverence he keeps watch at the heads of the loved one and the loathed one.
sentences.n: ‘Siteð ofer Bīowulfe’ is ‘sits over Beowulf’ (‘ofer’ with the dative, at rest); ‘byre Wīhstānes’ is ‘son of Wīhstān’ (‘byre’ nominative in apposition). ‘Eorl ofer ōðrum unlifigendum’ is ‘an earl over others, the not-living’; ‘unlifigendum’ is a dative plural participle, and I take the lifeless ones to be Beowulf and the dragon (a guess). ‘Healdeð … hēafodwearde’ is ‘holds head-watch’, the accusative of ‘hēafodweard’, with ‘lēofes ond lāðes’ (‘of the dear one and of the hateful one’), I take it Beowulf and the dragon. ‘Higemǣðum’ is a hard word. The manuscript has ‘hige mæðum’ in two words. Grein and others take it as the dative plural of ‘hygemǣð’, which they gloss ‘reverence’ (with a query); Sedgefield glosses ‘measure of ability’; Kemble and others read ‘-mēðum’ (Rieger takes it as a dative of ‘-mēðe’; Kemble, Bugge and Holthausen as a dative of ‘-mēðu’; the sense is ‘weariness’), and Sievers ‘-mēðe’, ‘weary-minded’, an adjective that would agree with Wīglāf. I keep Klaeber’s word with the gloss ‘reverence’, a guess.

sentences.t:
Nū ys lēodum wēn
orleghwīle, syððan under[ne]
Froncum ond Frȳsum fyll cyninges
wīde weorðeð.
sentences.l: Now for the people is expectation of war-time, after, openly, to Franks and Frisians the king’s fall widely comes to be.
sentences.i: Now the people may look for a time of war, once the king’s fall is openly known, far and wide, to the Franks and Frisians.
sentences.n: ‘Nū ys lēodum wēn orleghwīle’ is ‘now for the people there is expectation of war-time’: ‘lēodum’ is a dative, and ‘wēn’ takes the genitive ‘orleghwīle’ (‘orleg’ ‘war’ + ‘hwīl’ ‘time’). The ‘syððan’ clause says when: ‘fyll cyninges wīde weorðeð’ is ‘the king’s fall widely comes to be’, that is, becomes widely known (a guess at ‘wīde weorðeð’); the king is Beowulf. ‘Froncum ond Frȳsum’ are datives, ‘to Franks and Frisians’. The bracketed ‘ne’ of ‘under[ne]’ is Grein’s addition: the manuscript has ‘under’ alone, and Klaeber prints Grein’s form, so ‘underne’ is the word printed here, not the manuscript’s. It is uncertain. I take ‘underne’ as a spelling of ‘undyrne’ (‘not hidden’, so ‘openly’; ‘undyrne’ itself stands at 409 in an earlier part), but I found ‘underne’ with that sense in no source I could check, so ‘openly’ is a guess. The alternative is the manuscript’s ‘under’, a preposition with the dative, which gives ‘among Franks and Frisians the king’s fall widely comes to be’, that is, becomes known among them; the sense is much the same, without ‘openly’.

sentences.t:
Wæs sīo wrōht scepen
heard wið Hūgas, syððan Higelāc cwōm
faran flotherge on Frēsna land,
sentences.l: The strife was shaped hard against the Hugas, after Higelac came to travel with a fleet-army into the Frisians’ land,
sentences.i: Hard strife with the Hugas was brought about, from the time when Higelac came sailing with his fleet into the land of the Frisians,
sentences.n: ‘Wæs … scepen’ is a passive, ‘was shaped, was brought about’ (‘scepen’ is the participle of ‘scieppan’), with ‘sīo wrōht’ (‘the strife’, ‘sīo’ the feminine article) as subject and ‘heard’ (‘hard’) as its adjective. ‘Wið Hūgas’ is ‘against the Hugas’, the Franks. ‘Syððan Higelāc cwōm faran flotherge’ is ‘after Higelac came to travel with a fleet-army’: ‘cwōm’ is a variant of ‘cōm’, ‘faran’ an infinitive, and ‘flotherge’ a dative, ‘with a fleet-army’ (‘flot-’ ‘sea, ships’ + ‘here’ ‘army’). ‘On Frēsna land’ is ‘into the land of the Frisians’. ‘Higelāc’ is the spelling here and ‘Hygelāces’ at 2943 another spelling of the same name. This raid is the origin of the Franks’ hostility.

sentences.t:
þǣr hyne Hetware hilde genǣgdon,
elne geēodon mid ofermægene,
þæt se byrnwiga būgan sceolde,
fēoll on fēðan;
sentences.l: where the Hetware assailed him in battle, won it with courage, with over-strength, so that the mail-warrior had to bow; he fell in the foot-troop;
sentences.i: where the Hetware attacked him in battle and, with courage and overwhelming force, made the mailed warrior yield; he fell among the foot-soldiers;
sentences.n: ‘Þǣr hyne Hetware hilde genǣgdon’ is ‘where the Hetware assailed him in battle’: ‘hyne’ is the accusative ‘him’ (Higelac), ‘Hetware’ the nominative plural (a Frankish people), ‘hilde’ a dative, ‘in battle’. ‘Genǣgdon’ is Klaeber’s spelling; the manuscript has ‘ge hnægdon’, from ‘hnǣgan’ (‘bring low’), and Grein (with a query), Bugge, Holthausen, Sedgefield and Chambers read ‘genǣgdon’, from ‘genǣgan’ (‘assail’, as at 2204); the italic ‘n’ marks the change, and both words give a sense near ‘assailed’. ‘Elne geēodon mid ofermægene’ is ‘won it with courage, with overwhelming strength’: ‘geēodon’ is the plural past of ‘gegān’ (‘win, achieve’) with ‘elne’ in the dative, as in ‘elne gegongen’ (893), rendered there ‘by valor won’. ‘Þæt se byrnwiga būgan sceolde’ is a result clause, ‘so that the mail-warrior had to bow’, the mail-warrior being Higelac. ‘Fēoll on fēðan’ is ‘fell in the foot-troop’ (‘fēða’, as at 2497).

sentences.t:
nalles frætwe geaf
ealdor dugoðe.
sentences.l: not at all did the chief give adornments to the troop.
sentences.i: and the chief gave his troop no treasures.
sentences.n: ‘Nalles’ is ‘not at all’; ‘frætwe’ is an accusative plural, ‘adornments, trappings’. ‘Ealdor dugoðe’ can be read two ways, because ‘dugoðe’ (‘troop’, from ‘dugoð’) has the same ending in the genitive and the dative: ‘the chief of the troop’, or ‘the chief gave to the troop’. I take the dative, with ‘ealdor’ alone as subject and ‘dugoðe’ as the receivers; the sense is that Higelac’s treasure-giving ended with the raid. With the genitive nobody is named as receiving, and the line says only that the chief gave no treasure. Either way the chief is Higelac, who has just fallen; that is an inference.

sentences.t:
Ūs wæs ā syððan
Merewīoingas milts ungyfeðe. —
sentences.l: To us was ever since the Merovingians’ mercy un-granted. —
sentences.i: From that day on the Merovingians have shown us no mercy. —
sentences.n: ‘Ūs wæs … milts ungyfeðe’ is ‘to us was mercy un-granted’: ‘ūs’ is a dative, ‘milts’ (‘mildness, mercy’) the subject, and ‘ungyfeðe’ a predicate adjective, ‘not given, refused’ (a guess at the exact sense; Luick proposed ‘ungyfðe’ for the metre). ‘Ā syððan’ is ‘ever since’. ‘Merewīoingas’ are the Frankish royal house, the Merovingians. The manuscript has ‘mere wio ingas’; Kemble printed ‘Merewīcinga’, Thorpe and Grein ‘Mere wīoinga’, and Bugge and four other editors ‘Merewīoingas’. Klaeber prints ‘Merewīoingas’, whose ‘-as’ is the ending of a nominative or accusative plural, not of the genitive plural (‘-a’) that ‘Merewīoingas milts’ calls for. I render it as a genitive, ‘the Merovingians’’, because the sense needs one, and the grammar is unclear. The dash after the full stop is Klaeber’s: the speaker turns from the Franks to the Swedes.

sentences.t:
Nē ic te Swēoðēode sibbe oððe trēowe
wihte ne wēne, ac wæs wīde cūð,
sentences.l: I do not expect, from the Swede-people, peace or troth at all, but it was widely known,
sentences.i: I look for no peace or good faith from the Swedish people, but it was known far and wide
sentences.n: ‘Nē ic te Swēoðēode sibbe oððe trēowe wihte ne wēne’ is ‘I expect from the Swede-people peace or troth not at all’: ‘wēne’ is first-person present, ‘sibbe’ and ‘trēowe’ are accusatives, ‘Swēoðēode’ a dative (‘Swēo’ ‘Swedes’ + ‘ðēod’ ‘people’), ‘wihte’ ‘at all’; repeated negatives in Old English add up to a stronger denial. ‘Te’ is the manuscript’s spelling, ‘tō’ in Thorpe and most editors, ‘from’ here. ‘Ac wæs wīde cūð’ is ‘but it was widely known’; what was known follows in the ‘þætte’ clause of the next unit.

sentences.t:
þætte Ongenðīo ealdre besnyðede
Hæðcen Hrēþling wið Hrefnawudu,
þā for onmēdlan ǣrest gesōhton
Gēata lēode Gūð-Scilfingas.
sentences.l: that Ongentheow deprived Hæthcyn the Hrethling of life, by Hrefnawudu, when, out of presumption, the people of the Geats first sought out the War-Scylfings.
sentences.i: that Ongentheow took the life of Hæthcyn, Hrethel’s son, at Hrefnawudu, when the Geats in their presumption first sought out the War-Scylfings.
sentences.n: ‘Þætte’ is ‘that’ (‘þæt þe’). Its clause has ‘Ongenðīo’ as subject and ‘Hæðcen Hrēþling’ as object, ‘Hæthcyn the Hrethling’ (‘son of Hrethel’), with ‘ealdre besnyðede’, ‘deprived of life’ (‘besnyðede’ is the past of ‘besnyðian’, ‘rob’, and ‘ealdre’ a dative); ‘wið Hrefnawudu’ is ‘by Hrefnawudu’ (‘hrefn’ ‘raven’ + ‘wudu’ ‘wood’), a place-name. In the ‘þā’ clause ‘for onmēdlan’ is ‘out of presumption’ (‘onmēdla’, a dative) and ‘ǣrest gesōhton’ ‘first sought out’. Hæthcyn is the king of the Geats, Hrethel’s second son and Higelac’s brother (see 2432 and 2482). The endings do not show which of ‘Gēata lēode’ and ‘Gūð-Scilfingas’ is subject, since both are nominative or accusative plural. I take the Geats as subject and the Swedes as object, because the ‘ondslyht’ (‘counter-blow’) of the next unit presumes they struck first, and because the Geatish king is the one who lay dead; the other reading is possible, and the choice is a guess.

sentences.t:
Sōna him se frōda fæder Ōhtheres,
eald ond egesfull ondslyht āgeaf,
sentences.l: At once to him the wise father of Ohthere, old and awe-full, gave a counter-blow,
sentences.i: At once Ohthere’s father, old and wise and fearsome, gave him a blow in return,
sentences.n: ‘Sōna him … ondslyht āgeaf’ is ‘at once gave him a counter-blow’: ‘him’ is the dative ‘to him’ (Hæthcyn), ‘āgeaf’ the past of ‘āgifan’ (‘give out, give back’), and ‘ondslyht’ ‘counter-blow’ (‘ond-’ ‘against’ + ‘slyht’ ‘blow’). The italic ‘o’ is Klaeber’s: the manuscript has ‘hond slyht’, ‘hand-blow’; Grein (with a query), Rieger, Holthausen, Schücking and Chambers read ‘ond-’. ‘Se frōda fæder Ōhtheres’ is ‘the wise father of Ohthere’: ‘frōda’ is the weak form of the adjective after ‘se’, ‘wise’, and the father is Ongentheow; ‘eald ond egesfull’ is ‘old and awe-full’ (‘egesfull’ ‘fearsome’), in apposition to him.

sentences.l: cut down the sea-leader, rescued the bride, the old man the woman of former days, bereft of gold, Onela’s mother and Ohthere’s;
sentences.i: cut down the leader of the seafarers and rescued the wife: the old man saved the aged woman, robbed of her gold, mother of Onela and of Ohthere;
sentences.n: Ongentheow is the subject of ‘āgeaf’ before and of both verbs here. ‘Ābrēot brimwīsan’ is ‘cut down the sea-leader’ (‘ābrēotan’ ‘destroy, kill’; ‘brimwīsa’ ‘sea-leader’, an accusative). I take the sea-leader to be Hæthcyn, the Geatish king whom Ongentheow has just been said to kill at 2924–25; no name is given here, so that is an inference from the story; Kemble, Grein and Sedgefield print ‘ābrēat’, and the spelling does not change the sense. ‘Brȳd āhredde’ is ‘rescued the bride’; ‘brȳd’ here is the old wife. The manuscript has ‘bryda heorde’; Grein, Schücking and Chambers read ‘brȳd āheorde’ (‘freed’), Holthausen (first two editions) and Sedgefield ‘āfeorde’ (‘removed’), and Bugge (with a query) and Holthausen’s third edition ‘āhredde’, the verb ‘rescue’; the italic ‘red’ marks Klaeber’s choice. ‘Gomela’ is nominative, ‘the old one’ (Ongentheow); Kemble prints ‘gomele’, and Grein (first edition, with a query) and Lichtenheld ‘gomelan’, which would agree with the woman. ‘Iōmēowlan’ is an accusative (‘iō’ ‘formerly’ + ‘mēowle’ ‘woman’), ‘golde berofene’ ‘robbed of gold’, and ‘Onelan mōdor ond Ōhtheres’ ‘Onela’s mother and Ohthere’s’.

sentences.t:
ond ðā folgode feorhgenīðlan,
oð ðæt hī oðēodon earfoðlīce
in Hrefnesholt hlāfordlēase.
sentences.l: and then he followed the life-enemies, until they escaped, hard-wise, into Hrefnesholt, lordless.
sentences.i: and then he pursued his deadly foes, until at last, with great difficulty, they escaped into Hrefnesholt, lordless.
sentences.n: ‘Ond ðā folgode feorhgenīðlan’ is ‘and then he pursued the life-enemies’: ‘folgode’ is the past of ‘folgian’, which is mostly found with the dative; but the weak ending ‘-an’ of ‘feorhgenīðlan’ cannot be a dative plural (that would end ‘-um’), so I take it as an accusative plural (the house ‘ferhðgenīðla’, ‘life-enemy’), the Geats. In the ‘oð ðæt’ clause ‘oðēodon’ is the past plural of ‘oðgān’ (‘get away’), ‘earfoðlīce’ ‘hard-wise’, and ‘hlāfordlēase’ a nominative plural, ‘lordless’ (‘hlāford’ ‘lord’ + ‘-lēas’), because Hæthcyn lay dead. ‘Hrefnesholt’ is a place-name (‘hrefn’ ‘raven’ + ‘holt’ ‘wood’); I take it for the same place as ‘Hrefnawudu’ at 2925, which is a guess, since the text does not say so.

sentences.t:
Besæt ðā sinherge sweorda lāfe
wundum wērge;
sentences.l: He besieged then the great-host, the leavings of swords, weary with wounds;
sentences.i: Then he laid siege to the remnant of that host, what the swords had left, worn out with wounds;
sentences.n: ‘Besæt’ is the past of ‘besittan’ (‘sit around, besiege’), and ‘sinherge’ is its object. I take ‘sin-’ as an intensifying prefix (‘great, ever-’, as in ‘sinniht’, ‘perpetual night’), so ‘great host’; the sense of the compound is a guess. ‘Sweorda lāfe’ is ‘the leavings of swords’ (compare the house ‘homera lāfe’), the survivors, and ‘wundum wērge’ is ‘weary with wounds’; both stand beside ‘sinherge’ in apposition.

sentences.t:
wēan oft gehēt
earmre teohhe ondlonge niht,
sentences.l: woes often he promised to the wretched company the whole night long,
sentences.i: all night long he threatened the wretched band with woe, again and again,
sentences.n: ‘Wēan oft gehēt earmre teohhe’ is ‘woes he often promised to the wretched company’: ‘wēan’ is the accusative plural of ‘wēa’ (‘woe’), ‘gehēt’ the past of ‘gehātan’ (‘promise’), which takes the dative of the person, and ‘earmre teohhe’ a dative singular, ‘to the wretched band’. ‘Ondlonge niht’ is ‘the whole night long’, an accusative of time (‘ond-’ ‘along’ + ‘lang’).

sentences.t:
cwæð, hē on mergenne mēces ecgum
gētan wolde, sum[e] on galgtrēowu[m]
[fuglum] tō gamene.
sentences.l: said that he in the morning with the sword’s edges would slay, some on gallows-trees, [for birds] as sport.
sentences.i: He said that at morning he would cut them down with the edges of his sword, and hang some on the gallows-trees for the birds’ sport.
sentences.n: ‘Cwæð, hē … gētan wolde’ is ‘said he would …’ (‘hē’ is Ongentheow), with ‘on mergenne’ ‘in the morning’ and ‘mēces ecgum’ ‘with the sword’s edges’ (a dative plural of means). ‘Gētan’ is a doubtful word; I take it as ‘kill’, a guess from the sense. Thorpe and Sedgefield read ‘g[r]ētan’, ‘greet’, that is ‘visit with the edges’. The manuscript of the second half has only ‘sum on galg treowu’. Thorpe added ‘-e’ to ‘sum[e]’ (‘some’, plural) and the word ‘[fuglum]’ (‘for birds’), and Kemble the ‘-m’ of ‘galgtrēowu[m]’ (‘on gallows-trees’, ‘galg-’ ‘gallows’ + ‘trēow’ ‘tree’). ‘Tō gamene’ is ‘as sport’. The picture of hanging some for the birds rests on these additions, and the verb that ‘sume’ depends on is uncertain.

sentences.t:
Frōfọr eft gelamp
sārigmōdum somod ǣrdæge,
sentences.l: Comfort again befell the sore-minded, together with early day,
sentences.i: But with the first of day comfort came again to the sore-hearted,
sentences.n: ‘Frōfọr eft gelamp sārigmōdum’ is ‘comfort again befell the sore-minded’: ‘gelamp’ is the past of ‘gelimpan’ (‘befall’) with the dative, ‘frōfor’ is the subject, and ‘sārigmōdum’ a dative plural, ‘sore-minded’, the besieged Geats. The dot under the ‘ọ’ of ‘frōfọr’ is the metre sign explained at 2894. ‘Somod ǣrdæge’ is ‘together with early day’, that is, with daybreak (‘ǣrdæge’ a dative).

sentences.t:
syððan hīe Hygelāces horn ond bȳman,
gealdor ongēaton, þā se gōda cōm
lēoda dugoðe on lāst faran.
sentences.l: after they perceived Higelac’s horn and trumpets, the sound, when the good one came, with the troop of the people, to travel on the track.
sentences.i: when they heard Higelac’s horn and trumpets, the call sounding, as the good king came with the host of his people, following on their trail.
sentences.n: ‘Syððan hīe … ongēaton’ is ‘after they perceived’ (‘ongēaton’ is the past plural of ‘ongietan’), with the objects ‘Hygelāces horn ond bȳman’ (‘Higelac’s horn and trumpets’; ‘Hygelāces’ is the genitive of ‘Hygelāc’, a spelling of ‘Higelāc’ at 2914) and ‘gealdor’ (‘sound, song’) in apposition, the signal they heard. ‘Þā se gōda cōm … faran’ is ‘when the good one came travelling’; I take ‘se gōda’ as Higelac, a guess. ‘Lēoda dugoðe’ is ‘with the troop of the people’ (‘dugoðe’ a dative of company, ‘lēoda’ a genitive plural), and ‘on lāst’ is ‘on the track’, after the Swedes. The messenger’s speech goes on in the next part.
